title: In re the Detention of M.E. and R.S.
description: Whether the caseload limits in the Standards for Indigent Defense are mandatory and whether the trial court exceeded its authority in ordering the King County Department of Public Defense (DPD) to provide counsel in civil commitment cases despite DPD's capacity concerns.
plaintiff_argument: DPD argued that caseload limits are mandatory and the trial court's orders to provide counsel effectively forced them to violate these limits. The King County Executive argued it was prohibited by charter from providing counsel, as DPD has exclusive authority.
defendant_argument: Fairfax Hospital argued that caseload limits are merely guidelines and that the trial court has inherent authority to order DPD to provide counsel regardless of caseload limits.
decision_outcome: The court held that caseload limits in the Standards for Indigent Defense are mandatory and courts cannot order defense attorneys to violate them. It reversed the trial court's orders requiring the King County Executive to provide counsel, affirming DPD's exclusive authority. However, it affirmed the trial court's orders requiring DPD to provide counsel, finding that the trial court did not explicitly or implicitly order DPD to violate caseload limits.

title: State v. A.M.W.
description: Whether a court rule (JuCR 7.16) setting stricter prerequisites for juvenile arrest warrants conflicts with a state statute (RCW 13.40.040) on the same matter, and if so, which provision prevails.
plaintiff_argument: A.M.W. argued that JuCR 7.16 irreconcilably conflicts with RCW 13.40.040 and that JuCR 7.16, being a procedural law, should trump the statute.
defendant_argument: The State argued that JuCR 7.16, despite appearing procedural, was substantive because it limited the State's ability to enforce the Juvenile Justice Act, and therefore the statute should prevail.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that JuCR 7.16 is a procedural rule within the court's inherent authority and can be harmonized with RCW 13.40.040 by applying both sets of prerequisites.

title: Eyman v. Hobbs
description: Whether the Secretary of State has a mandatory duty to process a referendum on legislation that includes an emergency clause, and whether the legislature's emergency declaration for the legislation is valid.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Tim Eyman, argued that the Secretary of State's refusal to process his referendum violated his constitutional right to file one, contending that the plain language of the elections act and court precedent require the Secretary to accept it, and that the emergency clause in ESHB 1296, § 603, is invalid due to lack of sufficient justification.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, argued that he refused to file the referendum because the legislation was subject to a valid emergency clause, making it constitutionally exempt from referendum, and that as an executive branch officer, he lacks authority to override the legislature's emergency declaration.
decision_outcome: The court denied Tim Eyman's petition for a writ of mandamus, ruling that the Secretary of State had no mandatory duty to process the proposed referendum because the legislation contained a valid emergency clause, making it exempt from the referendum process.

title: State v. Sabra Danielson, State v. Simone Nelson
description: Whether individuals with invalidated convictions have a right to be reimbursed for all court imposed financial obligations, including labor performed in community service work.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that they have a right to be reimbursed for community service work performed to satisfy legal financial obligations after their convictions were invalidated, similar to those who paid cash.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that individuals with invalidated convictions do not have a right to be reimbursed for labor performed in community service work, only for monetary payments.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that Nelson and Danielson do not have a right to be reimbursed for community service work performed in lieu of legal financial obligations after their convictions were invalidated.

title: State v. James Ellis
description: Whether the resentencing judge's failure to consider Ellis's youth was an abuse of discretion and whether the restitution amount Ellis was ordered to pay violates the excessive fines clause.
plaintiff_argument: The resentencing judge abused discretion by not considering Ellis's youth, and the restitution amount was excessive, violating the excessive fines clause.
defendant_argument: The resentencing judge did not abuse discretion, and the restitution amount was not constitutionally excessive.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals on the resentencing issue, finding an abuse of discretion for not considering Ellis's youth, and affirmed on the restitution issue, finding it not excessive. The case is remanded for a de novo sentencing hearing.

title: State v. Evans
description: Whether King County's administrative booking process, which requires patting down, handcuffing, and detaining out-of-custody pretrial defendants to collect identifying information, violates article I, section 7 of the Washington Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the administrative booking process is authorized by law, necessary for jail safety and chain-of-custody, and that the privacy interests of pretrial releasees are similar to those who could have been arrested, thus not violating Article I, Section 7.
defendant_argument: Evans argued that King County's administrative booking process, involving pat-downs, handcuffs, and detention in jail, constitutes an unauthorized intrusion on the private affairs of out-of-custody pretrial releasees, violating article I, section 7 of the Washington Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's order, ruling that King County's administrative booking process, as applied to out-of-custody pretrial releasees, violates article I, section 7 of the Washington Constitution because it constitutes an intrusion on private affairs without authority of law.

title: City of Wenatchee v. Stearns
description: Whether a 911 caller's tip, combined with police observations, provides sufficient reasonable suspicion to justify a traffic stop for driving under the influence, with the City arguing it does and Stearns arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The City argued that the 911 tip was reliable because the caller was a bystander eyewitness reporting a contemporaneous DUI, and officer observations corroborated the report, providing reasonable suspicion for the stop.
defendant_argument: Stearns argued the traffic stop was unlawful due to a lack of reasonable suspicion, contending that the 911 caller's tip was not sufficiently reliable and the officer's observations did not adequately corroborate it.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, reinstating Stearns's convictions by ruling that the traffic stop was lawful.

title: State v. Mercedes
description: Whether Ferrier warnings, which require officers to advise property owners of their right to refuse, limit, and revoke consent before a warrantless search, apply to outdoor private property or are limited to a person's home.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that Ferrier warnings are not required for searches of outdoor private property, as these warnings are specifically limited to a person's home.
defendant_argument: Ms. Mercedes argues that Ferrier warnings should extend beyond the home to all constitutionally recognized private affairs, including outdoor private property, to ensure consistent protection for all privacy interests.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that Ferrier warnings are not required for consent searches of outdoor private property, and remanded the case to the trial court to determine if Ms. Mercedes's consent was voluntary under the totality of the circumstances.

title: State v. Nelson
description: Whether community custody conditions requiring breath analysis (BA) and urinalysis (UA) testing to monitor compliance with alcohol and drug prohibitions are constitutionally permitted under Article I, Section 7 of the Washington Constitution, even if the underlying offenses are not crime-related to drug or alcohol use.
plaintiff_argument: Nelson argued that BA and UA testing conditions violate his constitutional right to privacy because his underlying offenses had no direct nexus to drug or alcohol use, making the testing an impermissible intrusion.
defendant_argument: The State argued that BA and UA testing conditions are constitutionally permitted and narrowly tailored to monitor compliance with validly imposed community custody conditions prohibiting alcohol and drug use, regardless of whether the underlying offenses were crime-related to drug or alcohol use.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that Nelson's preenforcement challenge was not ripe for review, but also affirmed that the BA and UA testing conditions are constitutional as they are narrowly tailored to monitor compliance with valid community custody conditions, regardless of the underlying offense's connection to drugs or alcohol.

title: State of Washington v. Gator's Custom Guns
description: Whether Engrossed Substitute Senate Bill 5078 (ESSB 5078), which bans the manufacture, distribution, importation, and sale of firearm magazines with a capacity of more than 10 rounds, violates the right to bear arms under the Washington and United States Constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that ESSB 5078 violates the right to bear arms because large capacity magazines are "arms" in common use for self-defense and are integral components for semi-automatic firearms to function as intended.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that ESSB 5078 is constitutional because large capacity magazines are not "arms" and are not commonly used for self-defense, nor is the right to purchase them an ancillary right necessary for self-defense.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's decision, ruling that ESSB 5078 is constitutional and does not violate the right to bear arms under either the Washington or United States Constitutions.

title: Vet Voice Foundation v. Hobbs
description: Whether Washington's signature verification law for mail-in ballots, which can lead to some lawfully cast ballots not being counted, facially violates the state constitution's due process, privileges and immunities, and freedom of elections clauses.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that signature verification, by causing some lawfully cast ballots to not be counted, facially violates the state constitution's due process, privileges and immunities, and freedom of elections clauses, and seeks an injunction against its use.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that signature verification is a constitutional and integral part of the election system, is narrowly tailored to protect election integrity and security, and that its removal would compromise election security or necessitate more burdensome alternatives.
decision_outcome: The court held that Washington's signature verification law, when coupled with the expansive cure system, does not facially violate the state constitution's freedom of elections, privileges and immunities, or due process clauses, and granted summary judgment in favor of the defendants.

title: State v. McGee
description: Whether the state's attenuation doctrine allows police to apply for a warrant using tainted evidence when a new, independent criminal act lends new significance to the knowledge gained from that evidence, with the plaintiff arguing against such use and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: McGee argued that the July 13 warrant relied on evidence that should have been suppressed as fruit of the poisonous tree and that the trial court misapplied the state's attenuation doctrine, as the warrant application failed to establish probable cause without the illegally obtained evidence.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the attenuation doctrine allows police to use tainted evidence in a warrant application when a new, independent criminal act provides a new reason for its use, and that the superseding event only needs to occur between the unlawful police conduct and the prosecution's use of the tainted information.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals order, vacating McGee's conviction and remanding the case for a new trial, ruling that the attenuation doctrine does not allow for the use of illegally obtained evidence based on a new reason for its use.

title: State of Washington v. Luthi
description: Whether a criminal defendant may be required to appear for nonjury proceedings from an "in-court holding cell" without an individualized inquiry justifying such a restraint, with the plaintiff arguing against such a requirement and the defendant arguing it does not violate due process.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Cassandra Luthi, argued that being required to appear from an in-court holding cell without an individualized inquiry violated her due process rights by undermining the presumption of innocence, interfering with her ability to communicate with counsel, and violating the dignity of the proceedings.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Washington, argued that the in-court holding cell did not implicate due process rights, especially in non-jury hearings, and that any error was harmless because there was no jury and the courtroom was located within a jail building.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's decision, holding that due process requires an individualized inquiry before a criminal defendant can be compelled to appear from an in-court holding cell, and remanded for a new hearing.

title: Associated General Contractors of Washington v. State
description: Whether RCW 39.12.015(3), which requires the State to use collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to set prevailing wage rates, violates Article II, Section 37 of the Washington Constitution by conflicting with RCW 39.12.026(1)'s single-county geographic limitation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Associated General Contractors (AGC), argued that the newer law (RCW 39.12.015(3)) conflicts with the older statute (RCW 39.12.026(1)) because the single-county limitation applies to all data collected, including CBA data, thus violating Article II, Section 37.
defendant_argument: The defendant, State of Washington, argued that the single-county limitation in RCW 39.12.026(1) applies only to wage survey data collection, not to the newer CBA-adoption method, meaning no conflict exists and no constitutional violation.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that the newer statute (RCW 39.12.015(3)) does not violate Article II, Section 37 of the Washington Constitution because the older statute's single-county limitation (RCW 39.12.026(1)) applies only to wage survey data, not CBA-adopted wage rates.

title: Spokane County v. Meneses
description: Whether the Secretary of the Washington State Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) is a "state officer" under the Washington Constitution, thereby allowing the Supreme Court to exercise original jurisdiction for a writ of mandamus to compel DSHS to provide competency services.
plaintiff_argument: The Prosecutor argued that the Secretary of DSHS is a "state officer" under the Washington Constitution, allowing the court to issue a writ of mandamus compelling DSHS to perform its statutory obligations regarding competency services.
defendant_argument: DSHS argued that the secretary is not a "state officer" within the meaning of the state constitution, and therefore the court lacks original jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the Secretary of DSHS is not a state officer under article IV, section 4 of the Washington Constitution and therefore dismissed the petition for a writ of mandamus.

title: King County v. Abernathy
description: Whether a right-of-way granted under the 1875 Right-of-Way Act constitutes a conveyance "patented by the United States" under Article XVII, Section 2 of the Washington State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: King County argued that the right-of-way was patented by the federal government, meaning Washington disclaimed interest in the shoreland, and thus King County is the true owner.
defendant_argument: The Abernathys argued that the right-of-way was not patented, meaning Washington owned the shoreland at statehood and it is now owned by the homeowners.
decision_outcome: The court held that the right-of-way was an easement, not a land conveyance "patented by the United States," and therefore the land belonged to Washington at statehood and is now owned by the homeowners (Abernathys).

title: Bennett v. United States
description: Whether Washington's eight-year statute of repose for medical malpractice actions violates the privileges and immunities clause of article I, section 12 of the Washington Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Bennett argued that the statute of repose could not apply as a matter of law because it violates the Washington Constitution, specifically the privileges and immunities clause and the right to access the courts.
defendant_argument: The United States argued that the statute of repose was valid, that Bennett's cause of action was time-barred, and that the statute was supported by reasonable grounds and legislative compromise.
decision_outcome: The court held that RCW 4.16.350(3)'s eight-year statute of repose for medical malpractice actions violates the privileges and immunities clause of article I, section 12 of the Washington State Constitution.

title: Gonzales v. Inslee
description: Whether Governor Inslee's COVID-19 eviction moratorium was lawful and within his statutory and constitutional authority.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the governor exceeded his statutory and constitutional authority by imposing the eviction moratorium, which unconstitutionally delegated legislative powers, impaired contracts, constituted a taking, violated access to courts, and violated separation of powers.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the eviction moratorium was lawful, within the governor's statutory authority, did not substantially impair contracts, did not constitute a taking, did not violate access to courts, and did not violate separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' decision, ruling that the governor's eviction moratorium was lawful and within his statutory and constitutional authority.

title: State v. Reynolds
description: Whether counting an adult conviction for a crime committed as a juvenile as a "strike" for a mandatory life without parole sentence violates state and federal constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: Reynolds argues that imposing a sentence of life without parole (LWOP) based in part on his prior conviction for a crime committed as a juvenile violates state and federal constitutional protections against cruel or cruel and unusual punishments, citing the diminished culpability of juveniles.
defendant_argument: The State argues that Reynolds' current LWOP sentence punishes his current adult crime, not his prior juvenile offense, and that the "three strikes" law as applied to adults does not violate article I, section 14 of the Washington Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, upholding Michael Scott Reynolds, Jr.'s mandatory life in prison without possibility of parole sentence.

title: Snaza v. State
description: Whether RCW 10.116.030(3)(a), which requires county sheriffs to obtain authorization from the chair of the board of county commissioners before deploying tear gas to quell a riot, unconstitutionally interferes with the sheriff's core functions, or if it falls within the legislature's power to prescribe duties.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Sheriffs) argued that RCW 10.116.030(3)(a) is unconstitutional because it interferes with the sheriff's core function of quelling riots by delegating the discretionary decision to use tear gas to another official, violating Article XI, section 5 of the Washington Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant (State) argued that the statute does not interfere with a core function of riot suppression but merely limits the sheriff's use of one tactic, which is within the legislature's power to prescribe duties and does not constitute an extreme intrusion into county officer powers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, holding that RCW 10.116.030(3)(a) is unconstitutional as it violates Article XI, section 5 of the Washington Constitution by interfering with the sheriff's core functions.

title: Wahkiakum School District No. 200 v. State
description: Whether the "education" that the State has a paramount constitutional duty to amply fund includes school capital construction costs.
plaintiff_argument: The Wahkiakum School District (WSD) argued that the State is violating Article IX, Section 1 by failing to provide ample funds for school-related capital construction costs, asserting the State bears sole responsibility for such funding.
defendant_argument: The State of Washington argued that funding for school construction and other capital expenditures is governed by different constitutional provisions that primarily look to local school districts for funding assistance, indicating a shared responsibility.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision to dismiss the case, holding that the constitution does not include school capital construction costs within the category of "education" costs for which the State alone must make "ample provision."

title: State v. Teulilo
description: Whether Washington State's community caretaking exception to warrantless searches of homes is still valid after the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Caniglia v. Strom, with the petitioner arguing it is invalid and the respondent arguing it remains valid.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that the United States Supreme Court's decision in Caniglia v. Strom invalidates Washington State's community caretaking exception to the warrant requirement as applied to the home, making state cases recognizing a health and safety check exception invalid.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the community caretaking exception, including the health and safety check exception, remains intact post-Caniglia, and exigent circumstances still provide a valid exception to the warrant requirement.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision to deny the motion to suppress evidence, ruling that the warrantless entry was justified under the community caretaking exception.

title: State v. Rivers
description: Whether article I, section 21 and/or section 22 of the Washington State Constitution provide greater protection of the right to a jury venire drawn from a fair cross section of the community than the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing for a more stringent test for fair cross section claims and the defendant arguing that the existing federal framework is sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: Rivers argued that his jury venire and King County's jury selection system violated his state and federal fair cross section rights, proposing a new test for a per se constitutional violation or eliminating the systematic cause requirement under state law.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the existing Sixth Amendment framework (Duren test) is sufficient for assessing fair cross section claims and that King County's jury assignment areas were created to promote jury participation and diversity.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Rivers's convictions, declining to adopt his proposed state constitutional tests for fair cross section claims and applying the existing Duren test, under which Rivers failed to establish systematic exclusion. The court also affirmed the trial court's decisions on expert testimony and jury questions, but remanded for resentencing due to recent legislative changes.

title: Portugal v. Franklin County
description: Whether the Washington Voting Rights Act (WVRA) is facially invalid and unconstitutional because it allegedly protects some racial groups while excluding others and mandates race-based favoritism in electoral systems.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Franklin County's electoral system violated the WVRA by diluting Latino/a votes and that the WVRA is constitutional, protecting all Washington voters from discrimination.
defendant_argument: Gimenez argued that the WVRA is facially invalid and unconstitutional, claiming it protects only certain racial minority groups and requires local governments to favor some racial groups over others.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, rejecting Gimenez's arguments and holding that the WVRA is facially valid and constitutional, protecting all Washington voters from discrimination.

title: State v. Gonzalez (In re Sargent)
description: Whether "offenses punishable by the possibility of life in prison" under article I, section 20 of the Washington Constitution refers to the statutory maximum of the charged crime in general or the specific sentence the defendant is facing as charged.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that bail cannot be denied because the phrase "offenses punishable by the possibility of life in prison" refers to the specific sentence the defendant is facing as charged, which in their cases is less than life imprisonment under the SRA guidelines.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the phrase "offenses punishable by the possibility of life in prison" refers to the statutory maximum of the offense in general, not the specific sentence the defendant is facing, and all Class A felonies carry a statutory maximum of life in prison.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' decisions, ruling that bail can be denied for defendants charged with Class A felonies because such offenses are punishable by the possibility of life in prison, regardless of the specific sentence the defendant is facing.

title: Quinn v. State
description: Whether the Washington capital gains tax is a property tax subject to constitutional uniformity and levy limitations, or a valid excise tax, and whether it violates the state's privileges and immunities clause or the federal dormant commerce clause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the capital gains tax is a property tax on income, violating Article VII's uniformity and levy limitations, and also violates the privileges and immunities clause of the Washington Constitution and the federal dormant commerce clause.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the capital gains tax is a valid excise tax, not a property tax, and is consistent with all state and federal constitutional requirements.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's grant of summary judgment to the plaintiffs, holding that the capital gains tax is a valid excise tax and is consistent with the state and federal constitutions, and remanded for further proceedings.

title: Hanson v. Carmona
description: Whether RCW 4.96.020(4), a presuit claims notice statute, applies when a plaintiff sues a governmental employee in their individual capacity for acts within the scope of employment, and whether this statute violates separation of powers by conflicting with court rules.
plaintiff_argument: The presuit notice requirement does not apply to suits against governmental employees in their individual capacity because such cases are not against the sovereign state, and the statute violates separation of powers by conflicting with CR 3(a).
defendant_argument: The presuit notice requirement applies because Carmona was acting within the scope of employment, making the governmental entity the real party in interest, and the statute does not violate separation of powers as the legislature has the power to set conditions for suing the State.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals, holding that RCW 4.96.020(4) applies to governmental employees acting within the scope of employment even when sued individually, and that the statute does not violate separation of powers, remanding for summary judgment in favor of Carmona.

title: State v. Meredith
description: Whether the fare enforcement method used by armed, uniformed police officers on a moving public transit bus, which involved demanding proof of payment, constituted an unlawful seizure and disturbance of a passenger's private affairs under Article I, Section 7 of the Washington Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Meredith argued that the method of fare enforcement, involving armed and uniformed police officers demanding proof of payment on a moving bus without reasonable suspicion, constituted an unlawful seizure and disturbed his private affairs in violation of the Washington Constitution.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Meredith was not unlawfully seized, that his inability to leave the bus was not coercive, that he implicitly consented to fare enforcement by riding the bus, and that the government has a substantial interest in ensuring fare payment.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, ruling that Zachery Meredith was unlawfully seized by law enforcement officers during fare enforcement, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings with the instruction to suppress the resulting evidence.

title: Washington Food Industry Association v. City of Seattle
description: Whether the City of Seattle's ordinance requiring hazard pay for gig workers and imposing other constraints on food delivery network companies is valid under state statutory and constitutional law.
plaintiff_argument: Instacart argues the ordinance is invalid because it imposes an illegal tax on groceries, exceeds police powers, constitutes a regulatory taking, impairs contracts, and violates equal protection and privileges and immunities clauses.
defendant_argument: The City of Seattle argues the ordinance is a valid exercise of its police powers to protect gig workers and public health during the COVID-19 pandemic, and that the premium pay is not a tax.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed Instacart's claims challenging the ordinance based on the RCW 82.84 statute, equal protection, and privileges and immunities, but allowed Instacart's claims regarding regulatory takings, contracts clause, 42 U.S.C. § 1983 damages, and police powers to proceed to trial.

title: State v. Bagby
description: Whether the prosecutor's repeated use of the term "nationality" and other racially coded language, including questions about the defendant's dog, constituted flagrant or apparently intentional prosecutorial misconduct appealing to racial bias, thereby undermining the defendant's credibility and presumption of innocence.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecutor's repeated use of "nationality" and other racially charged comments, including questions about the defendant's dog, evoked racial bias and constituted prosecutorial misconduct, requiring reversal of his convictions.
defendant_argument: The prosecutor's use of "nationality" was incorrect but not an intentional appeal to racial bias, and was intended to help witnesses identify the defendant. The questions about the dog were to establish a witness's credibility.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision and remanded the case to the trial court for a new trial, vacating the defendant's convictions.

title: Washington State Council of County & City Employees v. City of Spokane
description: Whether a municipal ordinance requiring all collective bargaining between the city and union representatives to be open to the public is preempted by state law and unconstitutional under the Washington State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Union) argued that the City of Spokane's ordinance requiring open collective bargaining is preempted by state law (PECBA) and unconstitutional, as it conflicts with the requirement for good faith negotiation and a uniform bargaining process.
defendant_argument: The defendant (City of Spokane) argued that its ordinance is valid, not preempted by state law, and pertains to permissive subjects of bargaining, or that it is not mandatory and can be selectively enforced without conflict.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, ruling that section 40 of the Spokane City Charter, which mandates open collective bargaining, is preempted by state law (PECBA) and is unconstitutional under article XI, section 11 of the Washington State Constitution.

title: Associated General Contractors of Washington v. State
description: Whether Substitute Senate Bill (SSB) 5493, which modifies how the Department of Labor and Industries calculates prevailing wage rates for public works projects, constitutes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Associated General Contractors, argued that SSB 5493 is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority because it requires the industrial statistician to use wages from collective bargaining agreements (CBAs), effectively delegating legislative power to private parties.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Washington, argued that SSB 5493 is constitutional because the legislature made a policy decision to adopt the highest CBA wage rate and delegated the authority to identify and adopt that rate to the industrial statistician, not to private parties, and that adequate standards and procedural safeguards exist.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that SSB 5493 does not violate the nondelegation doctrine and is constitutional.

title: State v. Anderson
description: Whether Tonelli Anderson's 61-year sentence for crimes committed as a juvenile is unconstitutionally cruel under Washington's constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional based on a bright-line rule from State v. Haag, and the defendant arguing it is constitutional because Haag does not establish such a bright-line rule for all juvenile offenders.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that his 61-year sentence is unconstitutionally cruel, asserting that State v. Haag established a bright-line rule prohibiting any juvenile offender from receiving a sentence of 46 years or longer.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the plaintiff's interpretation of State v. Haag is incorrect, and that Haag only bars de facto life without parole sentences for juvenile offenders whose crimes reflect youthful immaturity, impetuosity, or failure to appreciate risks and consequences, which the plaintiff's crimes do not.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Tonelli Anderson's 61-year sentence, ruling that it is not unconstitutionally cruel under article I, section 14 of Washington's constitution.

title: State v. Sum
description: Whether, for purposes of article I, section 7 of the Washington Constitution, the totality of circumstances in a law enforcement encounter must include the race and ethnicity of the allegedly seized person to determine when a warrantless seizure occurred.
plaintiff_argument: Sum argued that he was unlawfully seized when Deputy Rickerson requested identification while implying car theft, and that his race and ethnicity should be considered as part of the totality of circumstances in the seizure analysis.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Sum was not seized until he fled, and that his race and ethnicity were not relevant to the seizure analysis in this specific case due to a lack of evidence of discrimination.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that Sum was unlawfully seized before he provided false information, and ordered the suppression of the false statement.

title: Bass v. City of Edmonds
description: Whether a city ordinance requiring safe storage of firearms and preventing unauthorized access is preempted by state law.
plaintiff_argument: The city's ordinance is preempted by state law, specifically RCW 9.41.290, which fully occupies the entire field of firearms regulation.
defendant_argument: The city's ordinance is not preempted because state law only preempts regulation in specific enumerated areas, and storage/unauthorized access are not among them, nor does it apply to guns in the owner's possession.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the city ordinance requiring safe storage of firearms is preempted by state law.

title: Kellogg v. National Railroad Passenger Corp.
description: Whether the 2019 amendments to Washington's wrongful death statute apply retroactively to allow new beneficiaries to assert claims despite a prior settlement, and if this retroactive application violates the state constitution's due process or contracts clauses.
plaintiff_argument: The 2019 amendments should apply retroactively to allow James' siblings to bring wrongful death claims, as the prior settlement only covered existing beneficiaries and did not waive future claims.
defendant_argument: The 2019 amendments should not apply retroactively because it would violate Amtrak's contracts clause and due process rights, as the prior settlement released all claims related to James' death.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that the 2019 amendments apply retroactively, allowing new beneficiaries to assert wrongful death claims, and that this does not violate the state constitution's due process or contracts clauses.

title: State v. Elwell
description: Whether the police conducted an unlawful, warrantless search of Daniel Ethan Elwell's covered object, and whether Elwell was deprived of his right to counsel.
plaintiff_argument: Elwell argued that the officer conducted an unlawful search by removing the blanket and plastic wrapping from the object, as it was not "immediately apparent" what the object was, and that he was deprived of his right to counsel when forced to proceed pro se on his motion to suppress.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the open view doctrine applied because Elwell and the object were immediately recognizable from surveillance footage, so Elwell had no right to privacy in the object, and that Elwell was not deprived of his right to counsel as he was assisted by counsel.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Elwell's conviction, ruling that while the police search was unlawful, the error in denying the motion to suppress was harmless, and Elwell was not deprived of his right to counsel.

title: State v. Bowman
description: Whether law enforcement's use of information obtained from a consensual search of a third party's cell phone to set up a text message ruse with the defendant violates the defendant's privacy rights under the state and federal constitutions, with the plaintiff arguing it does not and the defendant arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: Law enforcement's actions, including the consensual search of a third party's phone and the subsequent text message ruse, did not violate Bowman's privacy rights or constitute an unconstitutional trespass because the initial search was consensual and the ruse capitalized on lawfully obtained information without physical intrusion.
defendant_argument: Police needed a warrant or exigent circumstances to access text messages and impersonate a known contact, arguing that the ruse violated his privacy rights under Article I, Section 7 of the Washington State Constitution and the Fourth Amendment, and constituted an unconstitutional trespass.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals, reinstated Bowman's conviction, and directed the trial court to modify his sentence by striking the discretionary supervision fee.

title: Wash. State Legislature v. Inslee
description: Whether Governor Inslee exceeded his constitutional veto authority by striking a fuel type condition from an appropriations bill, and whether that condition itself violated constitutional provisions regarding substantive law in appropriations bills.
plaintiff_argument: The fuel type condition did not constitute a complete appropriation item subject to gubernatorial veto, and it complied with constitutional requirements for appropriations bills.
defendant_argument: The fuel type condition was a complete appropriation item subject to veto, and it violated constitutional requirements by amending existing law or being substantive law in an appropriations bill.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's summary judgment in favor of the Washington State Legislature, ruling that Governor Inslee exceeded his veto power and that the fuel type condition was a valid legislative limit.

title: State v. Peterson
description: Whether RCW 69.50.410, a statute criminalizing the sale of drugs, is invalid and unconstitutional due to implied repeal, desuetude, or violation of the state constitution's privileges and immunities clause, and whether its sentencing provisions conflict with the Sentencing Reform Act (SRA).
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that RCW 69.50.410 is valid and constitutional, and that its sentencing provisions can be harmonized with the Sentencing Reform Act (SRA).
defendant_argument: Peterson argues that RCW 69.50.410 is invalid and unconstitutional due to implied repeal, desuetude, and violation of the state constitution's privileges and immunities clause, and that its sentencing provisions cannot be reconciled with the SRA.
decision_outcome: The court rejected Peterson's arguments, finding RCW 69.50.410 valid and constitutional, and remanded the case for resentencing under the Sentencing Reform Act (SRA).

title: In re Williams
description: Whether the conditions of Robert Rufus Williams's confinement constituted cruel punishment under article I, section 14 of the Washington State Constitution, with Williams arguing they were cruel due to lack of basic necessities and assistance for his disabilities, and the Department of Corrections arguing they were not and had taken steps to mitigate risks.
plaintiff_argument: Williams argued that his conditions of confinement, including lack of reasonable access to bathroom facilities, running water, and appropriate assistance for his disabilities, constituted cruel punishment under state and federal constitutions, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, and sought release to home confinement.
defendant_argument: The Department of Corrections (DOC) denied Williams's request for extraordinary medical placement, stating he failed to satisfy community safety criteria. DOC also contended that Williams's violent offense and continued risk to the community justified his confinement, and that they had taken numerous steps to stem the spread of COVID-19.
decision_outcome: The court granted Williams's personal restraint petition, concluding that his conditions of confinement constituted cruel punishment under article I, section 14 of the Washington State Constitution, and directed DOC to remedy these conditions or release Williams.

title: In re Monschke
description: Whether the constitutional requirement that judges exercise discretion at sentencing, which forbids mandatory life without parole (LWOP) sentences for those under 18, also forbids those sentences for 18- to 21-year-old defendants.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that mandatory LWOP sentences for youthful defendants (18-21 years old) are unconstitutionally cruel, citing neuroscience developments that show no clear line between childhood and adulthood at age 18, and that these defendants should receive the same constitutional protections as juveniles.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the legislature's age of majority (18) is not arbitrary and should be respected, and that the court should not overstep the legislature's role in defining adulthood based on scientific studies, as individuals aged 18 and older have full adult responsibilities and consequences.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petitioners' personal restraint petitions, vacating their mandatory LWOP sentences and remanding each case for a new sentencing hearing where the trial court must consider the mitigating qualities of youth for defendants aged 18-20.

title: State v. Blake
description: Whether Washington's strict liability drug possession statute, RCW 69.50.4013, which punishes innocent and passive conduct without proof of intent, exceeds the legislature's police power and violates due process.
plaintiff_argument: Blake argued that the strict liability drug possession statute, which penalizes conduct without requiring the State to prove a guilty mind, exceeds the legislature's police power and violates due process, and that requiring her to prove unwitting possession also violates due process.
defendant_argument: The State contended that the statute is a valid exercise of police power, that the judicially created affirmative defense of "unwitting possession" saves the statute from unconstitutionality, and that declaring it unconstitutional would undermine other strict liability crimes.
decision_outcome: The Washington Supreme Court ruled that RCW 69.50.4013, the strict liability drug possession statute, violates the due process clauses of the state and federal constitutions by criminalizing wholly innocent and passive nonconduct, and therefore vacated Blake's conviction.

title: Woods v. Seattle's Union Gospel Mission
description: Whether the religious employer exemption in Washington's Law Against Discrimination (WLAD) is constitutional as applied to an employee whose job duties are not ministerial, given the employee's fundamental rights to sexual orientation and marriage, or if it allows religious nonprofits to discriminate without reasonable grounds.
plaintiff_argument: Matthew Woods argued that the religious employer exemption in WLAD is unconstitutional as applied to him because his staff attorney job duties were unrelated to religious practices, and it violates his fundamental rights to sexual orientation and marriage.
defendant_argument: Seattle's Union Gospel Mission (SUGM) argued that the religious employer exemption applies to its hiring decisions because all its employees are expected to minister to clients, and holding it liable under WLAD would violate its free exercise rights.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the summary judgment granted to SUGM and remanded the case to the trial court to determine whether SUGM's staff attorneys qualify as ministers under the ministerial exception, which would then determine if the religious employer exemption applies to Matthew Woods.
